# EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning

Mert Unsal Affiliation: ETH Zurich
Email: [mailmertunsal@gmail.com](mailto:)    Aylin Akkus
Affiliation: ETH Zurich Email: [aakkus@ethz.ch](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Building on recent advances in language-based reasoning models, we
explore multimodal reasoning that integrates vision and text. Existing
multimodal benchmarks primarily test visual extraction combined with
text-based reasoning, lacking true visual reasoning with more complex
interactions between vision and language. Inspired by the ARC challenge,
we introduce EasyARC, a vision-language benchmark requiring multi-image,
multi-step reasoning, and self-correction. EasyARC is procedurally
generated, fully verifiable, and scalable, making it ideal for
reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines. The generators incorporate
progressive difficulty levels, enabling structured evaluation across
task types and complexities. We benchmark state-of-the-art
vision-language models and analyze their failure modes. We argue that
EasyARC sets a new standard for evaluating true reasoning and test-time
scaling capabilities in vision-language models. We open-source our
benchmark dataset and evaluation code.

## 1 Introduction

A long-standing goal of artificial intelligence research is to develop
systems that can reason and answer questions about visual information.
Numerous benchmarks assess the visual reasoning capabilities of
vision-language models (VLMs). Previous work has created Visual Question
Answering (VQA) benchmarks where the model is asked (open-ended)
questions about understanding a real world scene generated synthetically
or created from real-world data \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] \[[7](#bib.bib7)\].
Other benchmarks include datasets of geometry problems with image
components \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]. However, these
benchmarks focus on extracting information rather than true visual
understanding and reasoning. In this paper, we introduce EasyARC: a true
visual reasoning benchmark inspired from the abstract reasoning
challenge ARC \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]. We believe EasyARC addresses a crucial
gap in multimodal AI: the ability to perform true visual reasoning
beyond simple information extraction.

![Refer to caption](2506.11595v1/images/ArcExample.png)

Figure 1: Example Task from EasyARC: The transformation is to identify
the largest connected component of non-background color and fill the
answer with the component flattened. All SoTA VLMs struggle to
understand or solve this example.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In [Section
2](#S2 "2 EasyARC Dataset ‣ EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning"),
we introduce the ARC challenge and consequently EasyARC with our
motivation behind creating the dataset. In [Section
3](#S3 "3 Evaluation of SoTA VLMs ‣ EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning"),
we evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on EasyARC, demonstrating that current
models fail on this very simple benchmark. Furthermore, we explore
[failure
modes](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Failure Modes ‣ 3 Evaluation of SoTA VLMs ‣ EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning")
of these models in an attempt to understand missing components for this
task and plot future research directions.

## 2 EasyARC Dataset

### 2.1 Original ARC Challenge

The ARC challenge introduced by [Chollet \[4\]](#bib.bib4) is designed
as a benchmark for abstract reasoning robust to memorization. It
resembles Raven’s Progressive Matrices where a matrix of figures are
provided and the test taker has to fill in the last missing figure.
However, in the [ARC
setting](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning")
we instead have a number of examples consisting of input and output
grids which entail a hidden transformation rule between them. In order
to demonstrate that the correct transformation rule was found, the test
taker then gets one or multiple test input grids and constructs the
output grid which is held against a ground truth.

![Refer to caption](2506.11595v1/images/ArcVisualExample.png)

Figure 2: Example ARC task from the public evaluation set: Visually,
this task is simple as it resembles stacking rectangles in a
three-dimensional manner.

ARC originally consists of 400 training and 400 evaluation examples.
Common approaches to ARC include (LLM-guided) program synthesis and
transductive reasoning with additional test-time-training
\[[10](#bib.bib10)\] \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. In both
cases training examples and test input grids are usually provided
directly in the form of language. [Li et al. \[10\]](#bib.bib10)
demonstrate that these two modes of reasoning are complementary for
solving the ARC challenge. Motivated by this, we investigate whether
visual reasoning can complement existing approaches to solving ARC
problems. This motivation stems from the observation that humans
primarily rely on vision to solve ARC problems. Some patterns become
evident in the visual domain but could appear convoluted when described
through lengthy natural language representations of the grid.

### 2.2 EasyARC

We initially evaluated VLMs on ARC, expecting them to generalize.
However, even state-of-the-art models — both open and closed-source —
scored near 0% when given only images. This failure reveals a
fundamental limitation: VLMs struggle with spatial reasoning and
grid-based transformations.

In order to facilitate a more meaningful evaluation, we developed
EasyARC with tasks that are similar to the original ARC challenge in
spirit yet require much simpler spatial/visual understanding. Since ARC
challenge has very small training dataset, non-vision approaches to ARC
often rely on synthetic data generation \[[6](#bib.bib6),
[10](#bib.bib10), [1](#bib.bib1)\]. Specifically, [Li et al.
\[10\]](#bib.bib10) categorized the 400 original training examples into
160 seed tasks, each annotated with human-written Python code for
generating examples, a natural language description, and conceptual
tags. Taking inspiration from this approach, we designed generators that
create tasks in three difficulty levels: easy, medium, and hard. Higher
levels typically require a superset of skills from previous levels. Due
to the combinatorial possibilities of grid sizes, color permutations,
shape positions, axes, and other factors, each individual task generates
a multitude of examples.

For initial evaluation, we selected five problem classes that cover a
diverse set of concepts:

- •
  Cross, Star: Introduces the model to basic geometric shapes on grids
  (e.g., rows, columns, diagonals) and their respective anchor points.
- •
  Counting Cells: Requires identifying and counting individual cells or
  contiguous shapes on a uniform background.
- •
  Double Grid: Involves copying a pattern while applying a horizontal
  flip or a color flip.
- •
  Dominant Side: Requires understanding sections of the image (e.g.,
  left or upper side). The transformation colors the entire image in the
  dominant side’s color while filtering out or preserving distracting
  noise pixels.
- •
  Drop One Color: Involves transforming one color into another while
  preserving a third unaffected color. The goal is to determine which
  color mappings apply.

We generate 1000 and 100 random samples for train and test splits from
each category, respectively. For all tasks, we sample from the easy,
medium, and hard categories with probabilities 0.5, 0.35, and 0.15 and
sample number of rows and columns uniformly random between 3 and 10
unless there is a specific requirement for a task. This results in a
diverse dataset of 5000 train and 500 test examples. We describe
detailed task descriptions in the
[Appendix](#S5 "5 Appendix A: Details of the tasks ‣ EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning")
with images included.

### 2.3 Benchmark for Test-Time Scaling of VLMs

EasyARC serves as an ideal test-bed for test-time scaling in vision
models. In particular, EasyARC is:

1.  1.  True Reasoning Benchmark: EasyARC tasks require multi-step
        reasoning, including hypothesis formation (e.g., ”Predict minority
        cell color”), iterative validation (e.g., ”But example 2 has a 1x2
        blue grid instead of a single color”), hypothesis refinement, and
        alternative perspective-taking.
2.  2.  Synthetic and Easily Expandable: EasyARC allows flexible dataset
        creation via configurable parameters such as grid sizes and
        difficulty probabilities. Our dataset includes 5000 training and 500
        evaluation tasks, which we will release alongside the generators.
        Additionally new generators can be seamlessly integrated.
3.  3.  Verifiable: Since the task requires an exact output grid prediction,
        evaluation is straightforward. This avoids reliance on proxies such
        as open-ended VQA, where complex multi-step reasoning tasks often
        sacrifice verifiability.
4.  4.  Gradual Difficulty Levels: We can adjust task difficulty
        progressively to provide a structured learning signal in an RL
        pipeline, allowing for insights into training dynamics.
5.  5.  Multi-Image Reasoning: Each example consists of multiple
        input-output image pairs. The model must correctly associate pairs,
        attend to their transformations, describe them, and generalize
        accordingly.

These characteristics make EasyARC particularly well-suited for
reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines where the base problem dataset’s
difficulty distribution is of utmost importance.

## 3 Evaluation of SoTA VLMs

In this section, we present our findings on the performance of SoTA VLMs
on our EasyARC benchmark. We evaluate closed-source models such as
Claude 3.7 Sonnet and GPT4o-mini as well as small and large open source
models such as QVQ-72B-Preview, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and
Gemma3-27B-Instruct. We pass a stacked image of input output grids as
well as a text prompt describing the task to all models. We use a low
temperature of 0.5 and collect 1 sample from each model due to budget
constraints. Despite the fact that our benchmark is designed to be
extremely easy, we find that all models except Claude 3.7 Sonnet exhibit
weak performance on this task, achieving scores below %20. We share the
prompt in the
[Appendix](#S5 "5 Appendix A: Details of the tasks ‣ EasyARC: Evaluating Vision Language Models on True Visual Reasoning").

![Refer to caption](2506.11595v1/images/successrate.png)

Figure 3: Success Rate of VLMs on EasyARC

We could not evaluate OpenAI o-series models extensively since the API
access doesn’t allow images as of the time we are writing this paper.
Through our manual evaluation, we expect o3-mini to score somewhere
between Claude 3.7 Sonnet and GPT4o-mini.

### 3.1 Failure Modes

To better understand the challenges faced by VLMs on EasyARC, we
manually analyze their outputs.

### 3.2 What Can Claude See?

Claude 3.7 Sonnet is the only model that demonstrates a degree of true
visual reasoning. To analyze its limitations, we break down its success
rate by problem category.

![Refer to caption](2506.11595v1/images/successrates.png)

Figure 4: Claude 3.7 success rate across problem types.

To interpret this plot meaningfully, recall that each category contains
problems sampled with probabilities 0.5, 0.35, and 0.15 from the easy,
medium, and hard levels, respectively. We observe that the model
struggles the most with Counting Cells, which requires precisely
counting connected components of a specific color. In contrast, it
performs significantly better on Drop One Color, where it simply
identifies a missing color, and Dominant Side, where it determines which
side of the image dictates the output color.

These results suggest that the model perceives a “blurry” representation
of images—capturing high-level features while missing fine-grained
details. Notably, most of its successes come from easy tasks; as soon as
noise is introduced or the mapping becomes more complex, its performance
deteriorates. This highlights a fundamental limitation in its ability to
generalize beyond simple pattern recognition.

### 3.3 Task Analysis: Counting Cells

Below, we include an example of an example input output for the Counting
Cells task, where the model needs to simply find the largest connected
component for the minority color and count the number of cells in this
component. All models, including the most successful Claude 3.7 Sonnet,
failed at understanding this transformation.

![Refer to caption](2506.11595v1/images/countingtask.jpg)

Figure 5: Example Input-Output for Counting Cells Task

The model usually identifies that the output should be of minority
color, which allows it to solve the easy version of this task. However,
the model is unable to look at the image ”longer” to realize that it
should find and count the largest connected component. This failure
suggests that test-time compute on images may be necessary, as models
rely solely on the training examples to infer transformation rules
rather than processing the image step-by-step.

### 3.4 Task Analysis: Cross/Star

While many tested models successfully solved the Cross/Star task, we
identified two notable failure modes.

The first failure mode is related to the model’s inability to precisely
locate objects such as cells, rows, columns, and diagonals.
Specifically, the model often fails to recognize that the highlighted
cell serves as the anchor point for the transformation. This limitation
appears to stem from two potential bottlenecks: On the one hand, the
vision component may struggle to establish a direct correspondence
between the cell’s position in the input and the placement of the
resulting row in the output. On the other hand, if the model was capable
of extracting precise positional information per grid in natural
language (instead of comparing them directly visually), it could
potentially mitigate this issue; however, our findings suggest that it
lacks this capability as well.

The second failure mode concerns the generation of diagonal structures.
Even when the model correctly identifies the transformation rule and the
orientation of the diagonal (e.g., upper-right direction), it frequently
fails to fully extend the diagonal. In many cases, the model only
completes the upper half of the diagonal after the anchor point while
neglecting the preceding portion. Additionally, some models generate the
diagonal in an incorrect position, despite correctly articulating that
it should be anchored at the given input cell. These findings suggest
that the model struggles with effectively integrating information across
modalities—specifically, transferring spatial knowledge from the visual
input to linguistic reasoning and subsequently applying it correctly in
the output grid.

### 3.5 Analysis of QVQ-72B-Preview Reasoning Model

QVQ-72B-Preview is the only reasoning model that was trained with
reinforcement learning to solve problems in our benchmark, in a similar
fashion to o-series models by OpenAI. When we look at the outputs of the
model, we realize that model has a clear mode of reasoning: even though
the model is supposed to do visual reasoning, it follows:

1.  1.  Extract the input output images into text.
2.  2.  Do text based reasoning to solve the problem.

Although correctly extracting the images is necessary to solve the task,
we also expect the model to mix the vision and language understanding
rather than using the image only for extraction purposes. We speculate
that this is an artifact of the model being trained on datasets such as
Geometry3k \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] where it is sufficient to extract and
solve the problem to get the reward. On the contrary, EasyARC presents a
benchmark where the VLM has to interact with the image and do some true
visual reasoning rather than mere extraction.

## 4 Conclusion

We introduced EasyARC, the first benchmark designed to evaluate true
visual reasoning in vision-language models. Unlike existing benchmarks
that focus on visual extraction, EasyARC requires multi-step reasoning,
hypothesis formation, and iterative validation. Our results show that
state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with even simple EasyARC tasks,
highlighting fundamental gaps in visual cognition. With its scalable
data generation and structured difficulty levels, EasyARC provides a
valuable testbed for studying test-time scaling and reinforcement
learning strategies in visual reasoning. We release our dataset and
evaluation code to foster further research in this direction.

## 5 Appendix A: Details of the tasks

### 5.1 Cross/Star

The Cross/Star task involves generating structured patterns based on
highlighted cells. The complexity increases as follows:

- •
  Easy: Given a uniform background with a single distinct cell, the
  model must generate a row, column, or diagonal anchored at that cell.
- •
  Medium: The model must create a more complex shape, such as a cross
  (combining a row and column) or both diagonals intersecting at the
  given cell.
- •
  Hard: Two distinct cells, each in different colors, are provided. The
  model must replicate the medium-level shapes while following a more
  intricate coloring scheme.

Key Concepts: Geometric structures (rows, columns, diagonals), pattern
formation, and color-based rules.

### 5.2 Counting Cells

This task focuses on counting and identifying spatial properties of
highlighted regions.

- •
  Easy: Given a uniform background and $`n`$ distinct-colored cells, the
  model must count these cells and output a $`1\times n`$ grid of the
  same color.
- •
  Medium: The grid contains clusters of connected components, and the
  model must output the number of cells in the largest such cluster.
- •
  Hard: The background becomes striped, making it harder to distinguish
  and count the target clusters.

Key Concepts: Object counting, recognizing clusters, handling background
distractions.

### 5.3 Double Grid

This task requires duplicating a grid while introducing transformations.

- •
  Easy: Given a grid with a background color and a pattern (dot or
  stripe), the model must duplicate the grid either horizontally or
  vertically.
- •
  Medium: The duplication is accompanied by a transformation, such as a
  180-degree rotation or a color flip.
- •
  Hard: A randomly generated $`3\times 3`$ grid must be replicated a
  variable number of times both horizontally and vertically, with
  transformations such as 90-degree rotations or background color flips.

Key Concepts: Duplication, transformation, rotation, color manipulation.

### 5.4 Dominant Side

This task involves detecting and analyzing the dominant portion of a
grid.

- •
  Easy: A grid is divided into two sides (e.g., left/right, top/bottom).
  One side (across examples) dictates the output grid’s color.
- •
  Medium: A uniform noise is introduced, requiring the model to
  distinguish the dominant side despite distractions.
- •
  Hard: The noise becomes more complex, containing multiple colors,
  while the model must still correctly identify the dominant region.

Key Concepts: Spatial division, handling noise.

### 5.5 Drop One Color

This task focuses on recognizing color transformation rules.

- •
  Easy: Three colors are chosen, with one always transforming into
  another while remaining consistent across examples.
- •
  Medium: Two colors are fixed, with one transforming into the other,
  while a third color varies across examples.
- •
  Hard: One color transforms into the background, with the background
  itself varying but making up at least 70% of the grid.

Key Concepts: Color mapping, background detection, transformation rules.

## 6 Appendix B: Evaluation

### 6.1 Prompt

We use the following prompt for evaluating VLMs.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The image contains a variable number of input-output demonstrations. To
ensure a unique solution, some tasks include more examples than others,
which can be flexibly adjusted in the generator functions. To guarantee
sufficient resolution for recognizing relevant details, the image
resolution was set appropriately. The model was also able to read small
annotations such as grid shapes and labels like ”Input” and ”Output”,
indicating that it had access to a detailed visual representation
sufficient for solving the task.

![Refer to caption](2506.11595v1/images/DominantSide4Demonstrations.png)

Figure 6: The goal is to predict the color of the lower side of the
image, not the majority or minority color. To guarantee uniqueness of
the solution we make sure to include diverse demonstrations.

## 7 Example Reasoning traces

In the following section we give an example for a successful and
unsuccessful reasoning trace to give some insight into the

### 7.1 Successful Reasoning trace

This reasoning trace belongs to a problem of the category counting cells
with difficulty easy. The model evaluated is Claude 3.7 and it correctly
understood that it has to count the number of minority color cells. A
common failure mode of other models was that they often only predicted
the minority color instead of counting, despite the demonstrations
clearly showing this rule:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 7.2 Unsuccessful Reasoning trace

This example shows an unsucessful attempt of Claude 3.7 to solve a
problem of the category Cross/Star task with difficulty easy.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This example illustrates a common failure mode in the model’s visual
processing: the model identifies the diagonal in the output as extending
only in a single direction (toward the bottom right), whereas it is in
fact a full diagonal originating from the anchor point.

### 7.3 Human Baseline

Another natural comparison beside the model to model comparison given in
figure 3 is the human baseline performance. Human labeling on our
dataset has not yet been employed, however human labeling has been
performed on the much more difficult ARC dataset which inspires our
problem categories and average performance was found to be between 73.3%
and 77.2% \[[8](#bib.bib8)\]. We therefore expect that the human
baseline is probably significantly above that percentage.
